newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish broad money, C/A seen under control.
newsitem.headline: Polish broad money, C/A seen under control.

text.p: Poland's money supply grew more slowly in October than a year earlier year and was in line with expectations despite fast credit growth leading deposits creation, analysts said on Wednesday.
Broad money grew 2.2 percent last month against a 1.2 percent rise in September and a three percent rise a year ago.

But credit for households rose 78.6 percent since the start of the year against a 36 percent deposit growth in the same period. In the first nine months of last year household credit grew 48.8 percent while household deposits rose 63.4 percent. @
"The jump in household credit signals high consumer demand and a weaker propensity to save and is inflationary," said Tadeusz Chroscicki, chief analyst at the Planning Ministry.
"In view of this data it seems a rate cut is out of question," he said.

But analysts said that even though the fast credit growth ruled out a rate cut, the central bank still seemed in control of broad money supply which grew 20.9 percent so far this year against 26.1 percent in the same period last year. @

"The money supply data does not seem to pose a major threat to curbing inflation because broad money is growing slower than last year and its source is domestic," said Krzysztof Bledowski, chief economist at WoodCommerz in Warsaw.
The National Bank of Poland said on Wednesday reserve money growth, its main monetary policy target this year through which it controls broad money, was within the target band in October.

Analysts said high domestic demand, combined with the lukewarm business climate on Poland's main export markets, was widening the trade gap by boosting imports and discouraging exports of goods which could be easily sold domestically. @

Since the start of the year Poland's trade deficit ballooned to $5.26 billion from a $930 million gap in the same period last year with cross-border trade inflows virtually flat at around $5.5 billion this year and last year.
The current account swung to a $358 million deficit in September from a $58 million surplus in August and compared with a $281 million deficit in September 1995.

But analysts said Poland may still finish the year with a deficit of between $300 and $500 million as a large part of the September deficit was seasonal and might not deteriorate much further this year. @

"September current account data is neutral and the balance of payments deficit this year is not likely to be high enough to be worrying," said Jacek Kuczynski, analyst at the Polish Development Bank SA.
Analysts also noted a large part of the high imports was investment which would help propel Polish exports next year and later by making them more competitive.
They were also not concerned with a dip in official currency reserves, those held by the central bank, because it was mainly a result of Poland's servicing of its foreign debt. @
Official reserves fell about $420 million to $17.55 billion in September.
"Polish reserves have reached a plateau after a steep 1995 rise and the September fall in no way throws them out of good proportions," said WoodCommerz's Bledowski.
